title: Upon Nothing: date, genre, tradition
short: A mock-encomium of Nothing, first printed as a broadside in 1679; Johnson thought it 'the strongest effort' of Rochester's muse.
body: The poem was first printed as a London broadside in 1679 and then in Poems on Several Occasions ('Antwerp', 1680); the archive follows the 1718 Works. It belongs to the Renaissance tradition of the paradoxical encomium, the mock-praise of an unworthy subject, like Erasmus's Praise of Folly. Johnson, who called it the strongest effort of Rochester's muse, noted a Latin precedent, Jean Passerat's 'Nihil', and observed that the poem's wit depends on treating 'Nothing' positively, as an agent, while sometimes slipping into the merely negative sense. Modern critics read it as at once a parody of the creation story, a sceptical metaphysical poem and, in its last stanzas, a political satire.

title: elder Brother ev'n to Shade
short: Nothing is older even than darkness, which in Genesis already lies 'upon the face of the deep' before creation.
body: In Genesis 1:2 darkness precedes light; Rochester makes Nothing older still, the first-born of all. Johnson wondered whether the line alludes to Wowerus's De Umbra, a Latin treatise in praise of shade which claims that shadow was prior to all things ('Omnibus umbra prior'); if so, Rochester trumps one paradoxical encomium with another. 'Thou hadst a Being e'er the World was made' parodies the language used of God or of Wisdom, who was 'set up from everlasting ... or ever the earth was' (Proverbs 8:23).

title: Triplets with alexandrine close
short: Seventeen stanzas of rhyming triplets, the third line in each a twelve-syllable alexandrine.
body: Each stanza is a triplet on one rhyme, two pentameters followed by an alexandrine ('And (well fix'd) art alone, of ending not afraid'). Triplets were unusual for a sustained serious poem in an age dominated by the heroic couplet, and the long third line gives each stanza a weighty, epigrammatic close, often the place of the sting. The form gives the mock-encomium a mock-solemn, hymn-like weight. 'Of ending not afraid' makes the point: Nothing alone cannot end.

title: primitive Nothing something straight begot
short: Creation out of nothing (creatio ex nihilo) told as a birth, against Lucretius's axiom that nothing comes from nothing.
body: 'Primitive' means original, first (Latin primus). Christian doctrine held that God created the world from nothing; Lucretius, whose De Rerum Natura Rochester knew and partly translated, insisted that 'nothing is ever born from nothing by divine power' (1.150). Rochester's poem plays the two against each other: Nothing itself 'begot' Something, as if Nothing were the creator, which is either a blasphemous parody of Genesis or a sly reduction of creation to absurdity. Critics differ on how seriously to take the poem's flirtation with materialist scepticism.

title: the great united--What
short: A deliberately vague name for the first undifferentiated mass, mocking scholastic terms for essence or 'whatness'.
body: The dash and the bare pronoun turn a gap in language into a joke: the first thing that came from Nothing is simply 'the great united-What'. The phrase suggests the primeval chaos in which everything was mixed and undistinguished, and parodies the scholastic quiddity (Latin quidditas, 'whatness', the essence of a thing), a term already mocked in the period as empty jargon. Editors note that 'Then all proceeded' makes this What the source of all particulars, a mock-philosophical genealogy.

title: must undistinguish'd fall
short: Everything that exists, cut off from its source in Nothing, must collapse back into Nothing, where distinctions vanish.
body: 'Something' is the 'gen'ral Attribute' shared by all existing things; Nothing is its 'sole Original' (only origin). The stanza predicts the end: all must fall back, 'undistinguish'd', into Nothing's 'boundless self'. Barbara Everett makes this cycle of all things returning to Nothing central to her reading of the poem as a grim metaphysical joke. The cosmology also recalls the Lucretian dissolution of compounds and the Christian end of the world, without committing to either.

title: Matter ... By Form assisted
short: Aristotelian physics, in which things are composed of matter shaped by form, retold as a rebellion against Nothing.
body: In the scholastic version of Aristotle, every body consists of matter (potential, shapeless stuff) and form (what makes it a particular thing). Rochester turns this theory into a family drama: Matter, 'the wicked'st Off-spring', escapes from Nothing's embrace with Form's help, and in the next stanza Time, Place and Body join a league against Nothing's 'peaceful Realm'. The political vocabulary of rebellion, leagues and realms anticipates the satire of the final stanzas.

title: rebel Light obscur'd thy rev'rend dusky Face
short: Genesis' 'Let there be light' recast as a revolt that dims Nothing's dark majesty.
body: In Genesis 1:3 God's first act is to create light, dividing it from darkness. Here Light is a rebel, and it 'obscures' (darkens) Nothing's 'rev'rend dusky Face', a witty reversal in which brightness eclipses darkness. The language of rebellion may suggest Milton's Satan, the light-bearer who revolts, though Paradise Lost (1667) is not a demonstrable source. The joke is that the whole created order appears as an act of disobedience against the original, venerable Nothing.

title: turn-coat Time
short: Time seems allied with existence but is secretly 'brib'd' by Nothing: everything it brings, it brings to an end.
body: A 'turncoat' is one who changes sides, a word given sharp point by the Civil Wars and the Restoration, when many changed allegiance. Time appears to assist Something (the Foe), but since all things in time perish, it actually serves Nothing, driving its 'Slaves' back into Nothing's 'hungry Womb'. The political metaphor makes metaphysics into a story of faction and bribery, preparing the satire on courts and councils later.

title: thy hungry Womb
short: Nothing's womb is also a tomb: the source of all things swallows them back, a paradox of a womb that consumes.
body: A womb should give birth, not devour. Rochester joins the two functions of origin and end in one image, as Job joins them: 'Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither' (Job 1:21). The womb-tomb rhyme was a Renaissance commonplace. Commentators point out that the paradox sums up the poem's cosmology: what came from Nothing returns to it.

title: Laick Eyes; the Divine
short: 'Laick' means lay, not clerical; 'the Divine' is the theologian, who alone is licensed to pry into mysteries.
body: 'Laic' (from Latin laicus, Greek laikos, 'of the people') means belonging to the laity (OED, laic adj.). 'The Divine' is a clergyman or theologian, who alone 'with Warrant' (authority) may inspect Nothing's bosom 'where the Truth in private lies'. The stanza satirises clerical claims to a monopoly of religious mysteries, with the insinuation that what the divines find, when they pry, is nothing. Rochester's deathbed conversion under Gilbert Burnet (1680) came after the poem was in circulation.

title: the Virtuous ... the Wicked
short: A double pun: Nothing takes nothing from the virtuous; and the wicked wisely pray for annihilation rather than hell.
body: The stanza turns on Johnson's distinction between the negative and positive senses of 'nothing'. 'Thou from the Virtuous nothing tak'st away' means both that Nothing does not harm the good and, cynically, that the virtuous have nothing worth taking. The wicked, facing damnation, 'wisely pray' to be part of Nothing, that is, to be annihilated after death rather than punished. The idea of preferring annihilation to judgment had libertine and Epicurean associations.

title: Great Negative
short: Nothing hailed with a grand title, parodying the 'negative theology' that describes God by what he is not.
body: The address gives Nothing the dignity of a divine name. In negative (apophatic) theology God is approached by denials: he is not finite, not mortal, not knowable. Rochester's 'Great Negative' turns that tradition on its head by making the negation itself the deity. The stanza then mocks the busy verbs of philosophy, 'Enquire, define, distinguish, teach, devise', which would be vain without Nothing.

title: to point their dull Philosophies
short: Probably 'to punctuate', to bring them to a full stop: philosophy's endless inquiries end in Nothing.
body: 'Point' could mean to punctuate a text or to mark its end with a full stop, and also to direct or give a point (sharpness) to (OED, point v.). The sense seems to be that without Nothing to put a stop to them, philosophers' inquiries would never end, or would have no point; their conclusions are always, in the end, nothing. 'Dull' sharpens the joke: Nothing gives point to what has none.

title: Is, or is not ... Ends of Fate
short: Being and not-being, truth and falsehood: the poles of logic and of Fate. In this text 'Fate' rhymes with itself.
body: 'Is, or is not' recalls Aristotle's principle of contradiction (a thing cannot both be and not be) and the Hamlet-like choice between being and not being. These are 'the two great Ends of Fate', and true and false the matter of all debate. In the 1718 text printed here l. 33 repeats 'Fate' as its rhyme, an identical rhyme; whether it is authorial or a printer's slip is a matter for the critical editions (Love, Vieth). The 'vast Designs' that these alternatives 'perfect, or destroy' lead into the political satire that follows.

title: sacred Monarchs should at Council sit
short: The satire turns to Charles II's court: why does Nothing let fools sit on the King's council?
body: The final stanzas turn from cosmology to politics. Kings sit 'at Council' (the Privy Council) with persons fit 'at best for nothing'. 'Sacred Monarchs' is pointed: Charles II's sacred kingship is set beside the worthlessness of his advisers, and readers in 1679, the year of the Exclusion Crisis and the fall of Danby, would have had candidates in mind. In the next stanza 'weighty Something' (substance, money, sense) 'modestly abstains' from princes' coffers and statesmen's brains, alluding to the court's notorious debts.

anchor: Lawn Sleeves, and Furs, and Gowns
title: Lawn Sleeves, and Furs, and Gowns
short: The robes of office of bishops, judges and aldermen, and lawyers or dons: dignified dress hiding emptiness.
body: Lawn is fine linen; the white lawn sleeves of a bishop's rochet made 'lawn sleeves' a byword for bishops (OED, lawn n.). Furs were worn by judges and aldermen, and gowns by lawyers, clergy and university men. Nothing dwells with fools 'in grave Disguise', and these 'rev'rend Shapes and Forms', the outward signs of authority, are what make them 'like thee look wise'. 'Forms' puns on the philosophical 'Form' of stanza 5.

title: French Truth, Dutch Prowess, British Policy
short: A catalogue of supposedly non-existent national virtues, all of which are 'seen in' Nothing.
body: An ironic list in the manner of the period's national stereotypes: French honesty, Dutch courage, Irish learning, Scottish civility, Spanish speed, Danish wit are all, the poem implies, nothing. French bad faith was a commonplace, and England had fought the Dutch three times since 1652. Rochester includes 'British Policy' (statecraft) in the list, so the satire comes home to Charles II's government and its secret dealings with France. 'Mainly' means chiefly, greatly.

title: King's Promises, Whores Vows
short: The poem ends with three forms of broken faith that all 'end' in Nothing, including the King's own promises.
body: The great man's gratitude to his friend, the King's promises and the whore's vows all 'bend' towards Nothing and 'in thee ever end'. Placing 'King's Promises' beside 'Whores Vows' was daring at a court where Charles II's mistresses were powerful, and where Rochester himself had been banished more than once for satire. The last word 'end' brings the poem round to its first stanza, where Nothing alone was 'of ending not afraid': the poem itself ends by ending in Nothing.
